title: A Man of Small Means Offers What He Can
intro: Abd Allah al-Salim ibn Hanbal, a scholar from what is now Mauritania, gathered reports of the Prophet Muhammad’s appearance and bearing into fifty couplets. He begins with a loss every later generation shares, the chance to see Muhammad for itself. From the gleam of a tooth and the feel of a palm, he moves to gestures and habits, ending with the way Muhammad found a seat in company.

translation: Praise to him who honoured the spirit of truth
with beauty of character and beauty of form.
1.sharh: “Character” and “form” are almost the same word in Arabic. The poet opens a portrait of the body by making room for the life it expresses.

translation: May the Maker of all creatures bless him,
the One who singled him out for the finest gifts.
2.sharh: The One asked to bless Muhammad is also the giver of the qualities to be described. The repetition of “Maker” and “creatures” links the gift to its source.

translation: Since we have missed the sight of the Prophet,
the highest thing to seek or desire,
3.sharh: The poet speaks for people born too late to see Muhammad. His “since” waits several verses for its answer, the collection he can make from other people’s words.

translation: and since his radiant descriptions
hold a distinction great indeed,
4.sharh: Accounts of Muhammad’s appearance acquire a particular worth for those who never met him. Arabic has a special form for wondering at greatness, and the poet uses it here.

translation: and the masters of tradition have set down accounts
so fine they make the bright stars blush,
5.sharh: The transmitters supply the material. The stars are made to blush as if they had heard a description brighter than their own light.

translation: I gathered them like jewels on a string,
to serve that most exalted presence,
6.sharh: Stringing pearls and composing verse share a verb in Arabic. The likeness explains how separate reports can be gathered into one act of homage.

translation: in rajaz verse I call A Man of Small Means’ Offering.
I kept out what would mar it or weary the reader.
7.sharh: The title makes the poem the gift of someone with little to give. Rajaz supplies a repeating pulse for a compact account meant to be learned.

translation: So I relate what the masters of tradition report,
doing my utmost to keep their words.
8.sharh: The poet promises to preserve his sources’ wording as closely as verse permits. The Arabic for “preserving” echoes the title for scholars who keep reports in memory.

translation: He was the fairest and most beautiful of people,
the most radiant and complete in form.
9.sharh: An overall impression comes first. The succeeding details will unpack what people could mean when they called Muhammad beautiful.

translation: He was imposing, well built, held in honour,
solidly fleshed without heaviness.
10.sharh: The first half moves from the impression he made to the respect people felt. The second gives the positive sense of fullness here, a firm build.

translation: His face was not excessively round, his head was large,
his build of a well-proportioned middle height.
11.sharh: The old descriptive terms distinguish a large head from an excessively rounded face. The word for his stature places him near the middle.

translation: Neither conspicuously tall, stretched thin and long,
nor short, his steps coming close together.
12.sharh: Unusual height and short, rapid steps mark out the extremes. The description gives proportion through what an observer would have noticed in a crowd.

translation: Even so, he stood taller than whoever walked beside him.
Far be it that anyone should tower over him.
13.sharh: After giving a middle height, the poet reports how Muhammad appeared beside a companion. His reverent closing words add to the sense of presence.

translation: He was bright and radiant,
fair, with a flush of red.
14.sharh: The light in the first half becomes colour in the second. The old expression “touched with” suggests a flush visible through the complexion.

translation: Neither chalk-white nor dark brown,
his face shone like the moon.
15.sharh: Two colour terms narrow the description before the moon brings it back to light. The account ascribed to Hind ibn Abi Hala specifies a moon at the full.

translation: A face as round as one could wish,
beauty flowing on through the lines of his brow.
16.sharh: There was a pleasing roundness short of the excessive fullness mentioned earlier. The lines across the forehead give the poet’s eye a path to follow.

translation: Liquid gold runs down his cheeks,
his sweat like pearls aflame.
17.sharh: The colour of gold and the shape of pearls give two different views of the same gleam. The pearls seem to burn as light catches each drop.

translation: The radiance of his lovely face puts to shame
the full moon on a brilliant night.
18.sharh: The comparison with the moon becomes a contest. Even a night giving the moon its fullest opportunity to shine leaves it outshone.

translation: Indeed, to see him was to see the sun
rising, and gladly do without its sight.
19.sharh: The observer turns from moon to rising sun. Once the face itself is visible, the sun that supplied the comparison can be spared.

translation: Whoever sums up his description says,
“I saw no one like him before or since.”
20.sharh: The poet yields the floor to an observer. A sentence about one person’s whole experience replaces the sequence of comparisons.

translation: At first sight he inspired awe.
Whoever spent time in his company loved him.
21.sharh: Time changes the observer’s response. The awe of a first encounter becomes love in someone who comes to know him.

translation: His palm was broad, his sinews long.
Anger made a vein stand out on his face.
22.sharh: A static feature of the hand gives way to a visible sign of feeling. The description attributed to Hind ibn Abi Hala places the vein between the eyebrows.

translation: His palm was softer to touch than silk.
His scent was sweeter than fine perfumes.
23.sharh: Touch and smell take over from sight. Someone who shook his hand could speak about him in a way a distant observer could not.

translation: His eyes were dark and wide,
his lashes long, brows distinct and arched, eyes touched with red.
24.sharh: A string of compact Arabic adjectives draws the eye, lashes and arch of the brows. “Ashkal” has been explained both as a touch of red in the white and as an elongated eye.

translation: His teeth were bright and spaced, his mouth broad.
His smile disclosed something like falling hail.
25.sharh: The small spaces between the teeth show when he smiles. Hailstones catch their cool white glint.

translation: His front teeth flashed, and from between them
something like light emerged as he spoke.
26.sharh: Al-Awadi gives two readings of what the onlooker sees. The light might be the gleam of the teeth themselves or seem to come from inside the mouth when the teeth part.

translation: His laughter was a smile, though sometimes
he showed back teeth like a string of pearls.
27.sharh: The ordinary smile and the occasional broader laugh are both remembered. The row of pearls recalls the image of stringing the reports together.

translation: He had a carrying voice with a husky note.
He spoke clearly, his words distinct.
28.sharh: A slight huskiness gives the voice a texture. Clear intervals between words make it easy for a listener to follow.

translation: The seal of prophethood he bore
by his left shoulder blade was like a canopy button,
29.sharh: The “seal” is a bodily mark described by early witnesses. A button from a curtained enclosure supplies one household comparison for its shape.

translation: or like a clenched fist, ringed with moles
like small raised marks that adorned it.
30.sharh: A second witness compares the mark to a closed hand. The surrounding moles help locate the feature more precisely.

translation: He had a head of hair that, if it parted,
he parted, and if it lay together, he left.
31.sharh: The old word for his hair can elsewhere name a birth sacrifice. Here the repeated verbs describe cooperating with the way the hair lay.

translation: His hair hung loose. He let it grow
to his earlobes and sometimes braided it.
32.sharh: The earlobe gives a visible measure for length. Braiding is remembered as one arrangement among others.

translation: It was wavy, without tight curls,
somewhere between straight and tightly coiled.
33.sharh: Three terms locate the texture on a scale from straight to closely curled. The middle term is the one the poet chooses.

translation: The white hairs in his beard and on his head
came to fewer than twenty. That too was part of his likeness.
34.sharh: The count is of individual white hairs. A small number allows the memory of an observer to be much more specific than a general description of age.

translation: His hands and feet were substantial,
his fingers long, his nose finely arched.
35.sharh: A substantial hand can still feel soft. The arch of the nose and the elongated fingers add finer contours to the portrait.

translation: His forehead was broad, his cheeks smooth,
his forearms broad, the bones below his elbows long.
36.sharh: This inventory moves from face to forearm. Arabic distinguishes the breadth of the arms from the length of the paired bones running down to the wrist.

translation: His chest was broad, his beard thick,
his neck like the neck of a sculpted figure.
37.sharh: A finely fashioned figure supplies the image for the neck. In the traditional account, the gleam of silver helps explain the resemblance.

translation: His joints were large, his upper back strongly built,
his bone ends prominent, his upper arms stout.
38.sharh: The unfamiliar words name parts of a frame, including the joints and the rise between the shoulders. The last detail puts flesh on the bones of the description.

translation: Bare-skinned, with a fine line of hair
and a graceful fold upon his belly.
39.sharh: The thin line runs down the middle of the torso. The old word for a fold describes skin as it lies on the abdomen.

translation: There was hair on his shoulders and upper
chest, and on both forearms as well.
40.sharh: The exceptions to the preceding description are the shoulders, upper chest and forearms. The metrical break falls inside the Arabic word for “upper”.

translation: So smooth were the tops of his feet that water ran
straight off them when it was poured.
41.sharh: Running water makes the smoothness visible. The portrait is about to turn from the tops of the feet to the arches underneath.

translation: His feet were high-arched, his shins
slender, his heels lightly fleshed.
42.sharh: The sole, shin and heel each have a separate descriptor. The “arch” is the middle of the sole that rises clear of the ground.

translation: When he turned, he turned his whole body.
He walked easily and at a good pace.
43.sharh: Turning fully gives the other person his attention. An unhurried manner is compatible with the ground he covers at each step.

translation: When he walked, he lifted his feet cleanly and stepped
leaning forward, as though descending
44.sharh: The weight moves forward with a decisive step. The poet lets the sentence run on to the slope named in the next line.

translation: a slope. He mostly looked in glances,
and a lowered gaze was one of his signs.
45.sharh: The slope completes the image of walking. An observer who noticed where he put his feet could also notice where his eyes rested.

translation: He turned his hands over when surprised,
pointed with his hand and turned aside when angry.
46.sharh: The gestures make feelings legible. A hand turned over expresses surprise, whereas the movement of the face signals displeasure.

translation: His face lit up when he was pleased,
as beautiful as a piece of the moon.
47.sharh: The moon returns when there is a reason for the change in light. This brightness is how someone looking on could tell he was pleased.

translation: He would often stroke his beard
when concerned about his community’s affairs.
48.sharh: The poet associates a small repeated gesture with worry about others. It is reported as a habit in these verses.

translation: Sometimes with a stick or a small staff
he traced the earth, keeping a thought to himself.
49.sharh: An observer could see the stick making marks but could not see the thought behind them. The line preserves that distance.

translation: He sat wherever he came to a place in company.
May his Lord bless him without end.
50.sharh: The last physical detail is a social courtesy, taking the place one reaches in a gathering. The closing prayer answers the blessing near the start.

1.2.2.head: خُلُق
1.2.2.meaning: Character or disposition, beside the nearly identical word for physical form.

2.1.3.head: بارِئ
2.1.3.meaning: The Maker who brings creatures into existence.

5.1.3.head: الحُفّاظ
5.1.3.meaning: Hadith scholars versed in both the wording of reports and their lines of transmission.

6.2.3.head: الجَناب
6.2.3.meaning: “The presence”, a respectful reference to the person honoured.

7.1.2.head: رَجَز
7.1.2.meaning: Rajaz, a metre much used for teaching verse.

7.1.4-5.head: جُهد المُقِلّ
7.1.4-5.meaning: “The offering of one with little”, a modest name for what the author can give.

10.2.5.head: مُطَهَّم
10.2.5.meaning: Excessively fleshy or puffy-faced in explanations of this description.

11.1.2.head: مُكَلثَم
11.1.2.meaning: Excessively full and round of face.

12.1.3.head: مُشَذَّب
12.1.3.meaning: Tall and slender, like a trunk stripped of branches.

12.1.4.head: مُمَّغِط
12.1.4.meaning: Extremely tall, as though stretched out.

15.2.4.head: الجَيلَم
15.2.4.meaning: The moon, also used of the first visible crescent.

18.1.4.head: الحُسّان
18.1.4.meaning: Very beautiful. Here the Arabic is a singular adjective describing the face.

19.2.2-4.head: طابَ عَنهُ نَفساً
19.2.2-4.meaning: “Be at ease without it”, willingly forgo it.

21.2.2.head: الخَليط
21.2.2.meaning: A companion who spends time with someone.

22.2.4.head: أَدَرَّ
22.2.4.meaning: Made something swell and stand out.

24.1.2.head: أَدعَج
24.1.2.meaning: Having large eyes with intensely dark irises.

24.2.2-3.head: أَبلَج أَزَجّ
24.2.2-3.meaning: With space between finely arched, tapering eyebrows.

24.2.4.head: أَشكَل
24.2.4.meaning: Having a little red in the whites of the eyes, also glossed as long-eyed.

25.1.1.head: أَفلَج
25.1.1.meaning: Having slight spaces between the teeth.

25.2.1.head: اِفتَرَّ
25.2.1.meaning: Smiled so as to show the teeth.

25.2.4.head: المُنهَمّ
25.2.4.meaning: Pouring down, said of hailstones here.

27.2.2.head: نَواجِذ
27.2.2.meaning: The back teeth, also used for the teeth just behind the canines.

29.1.1-2.head: خاتَم النُّبُوَّة
29.1.1-2.meaning: “Seal of prophethood”, a bodily mark near the shoulder blades in reports about Muhammad.

29.2.1.head: نُغض
29.2.1.meaning: A bony prominence at the shoulder.

29.2.3-4.head: زِرّ الحَجَلَة
29.2.3-4.meaning: “Button of a canopy”, a comparison for the mark’s shape or size.

31.1.3.head: عَقيقَة
31.1.3.meaning: A head of hair. The word originally denotes a newborn’s hair.

32.2.1-2.head: شَحمَة الأُذُن
32.2.1-2.meaning: The soft lobe of the ear.

33.2.4-5.head: سَبِط وَقَطَط
33.2.4-5.meaning: Straight and tightly curled, the two ends of the scale.

34.2.5.head: حِليَة
34.2.5.meaning: A distinguishing likeness or bodily description.

35.2.3.head: أَقنى
35.2.3.meaning: With a high, finely arched nose.

36.2.4.head: الزَّندان
36.2.4.meaning: The bones of the forearm by the wrist.

37.2.3-4.head: جيد دُميَة
37.2.3-4.meaning: “The neck of a sculpted figure”, finely shaped.

38.1.4.head: الكَتِد
38.1.4.meaning: The upper back between the shoulders.

38.2.2.head: المُشاش
38.2.2.meaning: The rounded ends of bones at the joints.

39.1.3.head: مَسرُبَة
39.1.3.meaning: The narrow line of hair down the torso.

39.1.4.head: رَقيق
39.1.4.meaning: Fine and slender. Another witness has daqiqa, with much the same meaning.

39.2.1.head: عُكنَة
39.2.1.meaning: A fold of skin on the belly.

40.1.3.head: أَعالي الصَّدر
40.1.3.meaning: The upper chest. The Arabic for “upper” continues across the line break.

41.1.2.head: مَسيح
41.1.2.meaning: Smooth-surfaced, here of the tops of the feet.

42.2.4.head: مَنهوشَة
42.2.4.meaning: Sparing of flesh, here at the heel.

44.1.2.head: قَلع
44.1.2.meaning: A clean lifting of the foot with each step.

44.2.1.head: تَكَفُّؤ
44.2.1.meaning: A forward inclination as one walks.

49.1.4.head: مِخصَرَة
49.1.4.meaning: A short staff carried in the hand.

49.2.1.head: نَكَتَ
49.2.1.meaning: Made marks in the ground with the end of a stick.
